chapter: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
title: Meeting Eleanor Roosevelt and Orson Welles backstage at Madison Square Garden
summary: At a benefit with Sarah Vaughan, Jones was quizzed by Roosevelt and Welles about how to accompany a singer.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Yeah. You had a recollection of Eleanor Roosevelt, I think you wanted to talk about.
Yes. I think -- this was a benefit at the old Madison Square Garden in New York, and you know how they have the buffet lunches backstage?
Uh-huh.

And I had no idea that these people would be there, because I just went to Sarah Vaughan, we were just going to do our act and play and get offstage, you know? So I went to get a bite to eat, and I'm standing in between Eleanor Roosevelt and Orson Welles. And at that point Orson Welles, he looked just about like he looked in 'Citizen Kane,' you know, he had that same look at that point, you know?
Uh-huh.
And what really got me was when I spoke with Mrs. Roosevelt, I didn't realize she was that tall.
Yeah, she was a tall woman.
And I was looking up at her. So I felt

like a dwarf, you know? And I had such great admiration for her anyway, her and Welles, you know. And the amazing part is their curiosity about the music business and how you accompany a singer of the calibre of Sarah Vaughan. They had evidently followed Sarah very carefully.
Well, I know that Orson Welles followed music, followed jazz, very closely.
Yes, he did.
But I never knew that Eleanor Roosevelt did.
Yeah, well, they both asked me these questions, you know? And I was honored to try to find an answer.
And they were both very knowledgeable about Sarah, is that right, or at least very familiar with her?
Well, I think Welles -- as you said, I think Welles was closer to it than Mrs. Roosevelt was.
Uh-huh.
But she was still like hungry for the information.
Can you remember the kinds of questions they asked?
Oh, let's see. No, it's hard -- oh, boy, this goes back awhile. It's hard to -- I may be able to give you the words to the effect that they said. How do you know
when she's going to do this, that or the other. Now, they didn't put it in those words, but I answered the best way -- you know, because you're talking from our industry to non-professionals.
Uh-huh. So how would you explain the answer to a question like that?
I would have -- you know, sometimes you have to become very elementary.
Uh-huh.
In your wordage, you know. Because we can talk, musicians or performers, we have automatic signals, you know.
Uh-huh.

Because we're in it. Just as they have automatic signals in their thing, you know. But I would say well, just -- if Sarah had an idea and as I once said before, we never rehearsed anything -- I would just follow it, you know, the best way I knew how. And the -- okay, I remember. The chemistry worked. We were a natural at that time.
Uh-huh. You had an affinity for one another musically, and probably the more you worked with each other the more you could anticipate, right?
That's right. And I could tell what she was going to do and she could tell what I was going to do. And, but Welles, by being in show business, he could understand, say
for instance if he's ad libbing on a line or something, you know, on stage, and suppose they forget a line, and somebody that's creative on stage, -- now he brought his conversation around that way.
Uh-huh.
You know. And then Mrs. Roosevelt, she just -- she was interested. She just stood there and listened. They were -- she was really just trying to appreciate American culture, you know?
